meta.title: What I've been seeing lately (in software)
meta.author: mei

comments.author: lumi
comments.text:
It's been great meeting more and more people that care, and seeing all of these communities pop up. Many people are sick of the tech industry but either don't know how to push back or are afraid to. We can lead by example! :3

I feel the downfall has been going for longer than GenAI, but GenAI is a fundamentally anti-social technology and has been significantly accelerating it. We are long overdue in having more people-focused tech, rather than corporate bs.

comments.author: marginalia
comments.text:
I feel the downfall has been going for longer than GenAI


GenAI largely feels like the spiritual successor to the grift culture that emerged with crypto, in ethos and very likely starting with a bunch of spare mining rig hardware looking for a new usecase after the crypto era lost the wind in its sails.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text: It is not even a successor, it is literally a project of the same people on the same resource base that were literally writing books that translate to plain words as «How to be a maximally abusive high-tech monopoly». This is not a fully disjoint crowd, but possibly a worse one, as these guys are much more quick than some of the crypto bros to buy governments directly to enforce their business plans on the peaceful population.

comments.author: sjamaan
comments.text:
Tech has been making me feel like I don't belong for a long time now. I'm one of the few people not on social media and still walking around with a dumbphone because the current smartphone duopoly is so unpalatable to me (and I'm afraid I will give into my internet addiction even more than I already do), and holding back on other "modern" tech like smart home stuff. Now this LLM craze is coming in and I see myself resisting yet again and many smart people who I respect falling for it.

It's nice to see at least some people still care but I also feel it's a losing battle and we'll all be swept away by the tide. I worry for my kids who have to live in this society where all this garbage is normalized.

I miss positive alternatives :(

comments.author: lumi
comments.text: The good thing is that positivity is contagious and many people feel the way you do! Together we can improve things, we can resist antisocial and unethical tech like LLMs.

comments.author: sjamaan
comments.text: A glimmer of light is that at least here on lobste.rs a majority of people seem to be at least somewhat AI-sceptical, and the discussion seems to become more productive.

comments.author: lumi
comments.text: Yup! And we should strive to shift the opinion window everywhere to be more and more hostile to GenAI! :)

comments.author: mxuribe
comments.text:
Hi @mei thanks for posting this! I've seen, felt something similar! I've been meaning to craft a blog post myself to spit out some of the thoughts I've had on this topic...So, you've given me some motivation.

As a bit of a preview, with all the stuff that has been happening, it sure feels like this internet is not our internet. There was at first the arpanet, then the early internet (along with webs 1.0 and 2.0), and now we have the modern internet (including its not-so-great web and its not-so-great social networks)...so what comes next is what i'll say is post-modern; the postnet (or posternet). I envision a return to smaller communities (like tilde communities), less static/more signal, deeper engagement, but also offline stuff. From the outside, things will appear to have slowed down, but in reality its a way of engaging with other humans that is more deliberate, perhaps enriching in more positive ways. More thoughts soon to come...

comments.author: mempko
comments.text:
I've been coding for 30 years. I've felt like an alien in the tech community for a long time, especially what comes out of the valley. And again I'm going to say something controversial so here goes.

Prior to LLMs software quality across the board, corporate and open source was shit. The software community failed humanity as they relied on our work to run the modern world. This gave us great privilege and also complacency. There were of course pockets of greatness, but on the whole I feel as an industry we failed.

Only 5% of time building software is writing code and now LLMs are good enough at it that people no longer need to rely on that low level skill. However they still need us for complex systems.

The average complexity of software is going to increase and I'm afraid the industry will just continue the slop but at a greater scale.

At the same time LLMs are allowing new people with new thinking to enter the community and we should welcome them. Why? Because thinking has been stagnant in the software world for awhile.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
There were of course pockets of greatness, but on the whole I feel as an industry we failed.


Has there been any industry that was not busy failing humanity until product liability got teeth?

comments.author: mempko
comments.text: Probably not and that's a good point. If you compare our discipline to others it's pretty new. It's just a baby compared to say other engineering disciplines, architecture, etc.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
It's kind of a good point to drastically restrict liability disclaimers in software brought to the market (slightly more narrow than published — excludes open enough stuff) by companies larger than some income / investment / asset threshold. Every word Microsoft says about infeasibility of fixing a bug should go immediately into the case about false advertisement of Copilot.

Of course, one could imagine intermediate steps. If you protect it, you consider it worth protecting. So every issue that the vendor has prevented others from fixing (technical or legal means) and did not promptly fix (industry best practices say 90 days?) gives ground to unlimited product liability, no disclaimers. Let's say ten years after release as the target, with gradual phase-in.

comments.author: jscancella
comments.text:
Prior to LLMs software quality across the board, corporate and open source was shit.


The interesting question to me is why is that? I tend to believe it is because software is still seen as a cost center (to be minimized) instead of an enabler or core competency (needing investment and care). I see it every day where the business people tell me "just do whatever is easiest (read cheapest)". Or when my management tells me to do a complete migration from our data center to a cloud provider in an unreasonable amount of time and limited resources.

If things that other engineers built took this same approach, you would have the same shitty outcomes. TL;DR - software is terrible because people don't want to pay for quality when mediocre will do, and then it is a race to the bottom.

comments.author: gkoos
comments.text:
I don't want to get dragged into the mud, but imagine someone in 1995 saying, "We have C, Unix, relational databases, and TCP/IP. That's plenty. Let's stop".
A healthy engineering culture should be able to find some middle ground between "this new thing is rubbish, don't touch it" and "this just has solved computer science, bro".
